stories.title: Lok Sabha passes bill to expand the Supreme Court from 34 to 38 judges — with almost no debate
key_points: The Lok Sabha passed the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026**, raising the court's total sanctioned strength — including the Chief Justice of India — from **34 to 38 judges**.
The bill passed with **almost no debate**, as opposition MPs were occupied protesting inside the House.
Opposition protests centered on **police action against student protesters at Jantar Mantar** in Delhi and reports of **irregularities at the Ram Temple trust** in Ayodhya.
The same day, the Rajya Sabha separately passed the **MSME Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026**.
The government's stated reason for expanding the court is to tackle India's large and growing **case pendency** backlog.
stories.background: The Supreme Court of India's sanctioned strength — how many judges it's legally allowed to have, separate from how many seats are actually filled — has been raised by Parliament several times before as the court's caseload has grown; it was last increased in 2019, from 31 to 34 judges including the CJI. India's top court faces a well-documented backlog of tens of thousands of pending cases, repeatedly cited as justification for adding judges. This bill still needs to pass the Rajya Sabha and receive presidential assent before it takes effect.
stories.what_happened: On Monday, August 3, the Lok Sabha passed the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026**, raising the sanctioned strength of Supreme Court judges from **33 to 37** — meaning the total court size, including the Chief Justice of India, rises from **34 to 38**. The bill passed with virtually no floor debate because opposition members were preoccupied with protests inside the House, linked to two separate controversies: police action against student protesters at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, and reports of irregularities connected to the Ram Temple trust in Ayodhya. On the same day, the Rajya Sabha passed a separate, unrelated bill — the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026.
stories.why_it_matters: More sanctioned judge seats means the Supreme Court can, in theory, hear more cases and chip away faster at its backlog — a structural fix to a decades-old capacity problem. But passing a significant judiciary-reshaping bill with essentially zero debate, amid unrelated protests drowning out scrutiny, is itself notable for how India's Parliament is currently functioning.
stories.ripple_effects: A larger sanctioned bench eventually means more judicial appointments to fill, putting the spotlight on the Collegium — the body of senior judges that recommends who gets appointed — and could reignite debate over how judges are chosen. It may take months to years for the extra seats to actually be filled.
stories.why_now: The bill moved forward as part of the ongoing Monsoon Session of Parliament, but it passed quickly and quietly because opposition attention was consumed by the Jantar Mantar and Ram Temple controversies playing out in the same session.
stories.watch_next: Whether the bill clears the Rajya Sabha and gets presidential assent, and how quickly the government moves to nominate judges for the four new seats.

key_terms.definition: The maximum number of judges a court is legally allowed to have at once, as set by Parliament — separate from how many of those seats are currently filled.

stories.the_lesson: Watch not just what a legislature passes, but how — a major structural change to an institution like the judiciary can move through with almost no public debate when attention is captured elsewhere in the same session.

stories.title: RBI set to hold interest rates steady on August 5 as it weighs Middle East oil risk against a stabilizing rupee
key_points: The RBI's six-member Monetary Policy Committee, led by Governor **Sanjay Malhotra**, is widely expected to hold its key repo rate at **5.25%** when it announces its decision on **Wednesday, August 5**.
**29 of 30 economists** surveyed by Bloomberg expect no change in rates.
Retail inflation was **4.38% in June**, still comfortably inside the RBI's tolerance band, but policymakers are watching for oil-driven price spillover.
The renewed Middle East conflict has pushed up energy costs, a key upside risk to inflation the RBI wants to see play out before moving rates either way.
**$40 billion** in fresh forex inflows — driven by a scrapped capital-gains tax and attractive dollar deposit schemes — have helped stabilize the rupee without needing a rate hike.
stories.background: India's central bank sets its benchmark 'repo rate' — the interest rate at which it lends to commercial banks — roughly every two months through its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), a six-member panel that votes on the decision. The RBI balances two competing goals: keeping inflation low (its mandate is roughly 4%, with a 2-6% tolerance band) and supporting growth by keeping borrowing affordable. Since the Middle East conflict escalated, oil-importing India has faced higher energy import costs, historically one of the biggest inflation risks for the Indian economy given how much fuel and transport costs feed into broader prices.
stories.what_happened: Indian stock markets have been trading with a cautious, positive bias ahead of the RBI's rate decision, due Wednesday, August 5. The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Governor Sanjay Malhotra, is expected by nearly the entire community of forecasters — 29 of 30 economists surveyed by Bloomberg — to keep the repo rate unchanged at **5.25%**. The case for holding: retail inflation was a moderate 4.38% in June, within the RBI's comfort zone, and roughly **$40 billion** in new foreign exchange inflows — thanks to India scrapping capital-gains tax on certain investments and offering attractive dollar-deposit schemes — have helped stabilize the rupee without the RBI needing to raise rates to defend it. The case for caution: the renewed Middle East conflict, including the Strait of Hormuz tensions and Iran standoff, has pushed oil prices higher, and the RBI wants to see whether that cost passes through into broader inflation before it commits to its next move.
stories.why_it_matters: The repo rate directly shapes how expensive loans are for Indian households and businesses — mortgages, car loans, and business credit all move with it. Holding steady signals the RBI thinks the economy doesn't need a fresh boost right now, but also isn't worried enough about oil-driven inflation to hike.
stories.ripple_effects: A hold is broadly priced in, so the bigger market-mover will be the RBI's tone: any hint of concern about oil-driven inflation could weigh on bond prices and the rupee, while a confident, growth-supportive tone could extend the recent rally in Sensex and Nifty.
stories.why_now: The decision lands at a delicate moment — Middle East oil risk is rising just as India's forex position has quietly improved, giving the RBI more room to wait and watch rather than react.
stories.watch_next: The RBI's official decision and Governor Malhotra's press conference on Wednesday, August 5, including any change in language about inflation risk from the Middle East conflict.

key_terms.definition: The interest rate at which India's central bank lends short-term money to commercial banks — when it goes up, loans across the economy generally get more expensive, and vice versa.

stories.the_lesson: Central banks don't just react to current inflation numbers — they try to look through temporary shocks, like an oil-price spike from a war, to the underlying trend, which is why a rate decision can stay unchanged even when a real inflation risk is visibly building.
stories.market_link: Directly moves Indian bond yields, the rupee, and rate-sensitive stocks (banks, NBFCs, real estate, autos) — a hold as expected should be a non-event, but any hawkish tone shift is the real risk for Sensex/Nifty this week.

stories.title: ONGC's profit more than doubles to ₹17,034 crore as the Middle East conflict pushes up what it earns per barrel of oil
key_points: **ONGC's** net profit surged **112%** year-on-year to **₹17,033.81 crore** in the June quarter (Q1 FY27)
Profit before tax hit a **record quarterly high of ₹22,848 crore**
Total income rose to **₹48,321.65 crore**, up from ₹33,213.39 crore a year earlier
Net crude oil realisation jumped to **₹99.45 a barrel**, from ₹66.13 a year ago
The jump was driven by **higher global crude prices**, not higher production volumes
stories.background: **ONGC (Oil and Natural Gas Corporation)** is India's largest state-run oil and gas explorer, and its profits move closely with global crude oil prices since it sells the oil and gas it pumps at prevailing market rates. A year ago, in Q1 FY26, ONGC's profit was much lower at ₹8,024 crore because oil prices were weaker then. Crude prices have climbed sharply through 2026 amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, including attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz and the broader Iran standoff — both of which have been rattling global energy markets.
stories.what_happened: ONGC reported **Q1 FY27 (April-June 2026) net profit of ₹17,033.81 crore**, more than double the ₹8,024.23 crore it made in the same quarter last year, and also well above the ₹6,649.97 crore it posted in the previous (January-March) quarter. The company's **profit before tax hit a record ₹22,848 crore** for a single quarter. Total income rose to ₹48,321.65 crore from ₹33,213.39 crore a year earlier. The key driver was price, not volume: ONGC's **net crude oil realisation** — what it actually earns per barrel after costs — rose to ₹99.45 from ₹66.13 a year ago, tracking the rise in global oil prices.
stories.why_it_matters: As a government-owned company, ONGC's profits flow partly back to the exchequer through dividends and taxes, so a stronger quarter helps India's public finances. It's also a direct read on how the Middle East conflict is reshaping costs and profits across the energy sector — a cost for fuel-importing consumers and businesses, but a windfall for a producer like ONGC.
stories.ripple_effects: Higher crude realisations are good news for ONGC shareholders and the government's dividend income, but the same rising oil prices squeeze India's refiners, airlines, and consumers who pay more at the pump. It also reinforces why India's policymakers are closely watching the Strait of Hormuz situation, since further escalation there would push ONGC's realisations — and the cost of oil for everyone else — even higher.
stories.why_now: Q1 FY27 results were scheduled for release on August 4 as part of India's quarterly corporate earnings season, alongside dozens of other companies reporting the same day.
stories.watch_next: Whether crude prices stay elevated through Q2, and how much of this profit ONGC returns to shareholders via dividends.

key_terms.definition: The actual price a company like ONGC pockets per barrel of oil after subsidies, discounts, and costs — different from the quoted global crude price.

stories.the_lesson: The same global event can be a windfall for producers and a burden for consumers at the same time — rising oil prices simultaneously boost an oil company's profit and raise costs for everyone who buys fuel.
stories.market_link: ONGC shares react directly to this result; the broader story ties to crude oil prices, which move on Middle East/Strait of Hormuz tensions and affect Indian refiners, airlines, and the rupee via the import bill.

stories.title: India says trade talks with the US are still 'ongoing' — six months after Trump and Modi announced a tariff-cutting deal
key_points: MEA spokesperson **Randhir Jaiswal** confirmed talks on an **interim bilateral trade agreement** are still ongoing
Both sides have done **'a lot of work'**, but no final deal has been signed yet
In **February 2026**, Trump and Modi announced a deal cutting US tariffs on Indian goods from **25% to 18%**
Separately, **25 US states** are suing the Trump administration over broader tariffs that include India in a **10% bracket**
The comments came at the MEA's routine **bi-weekly media briefing** in New Delhi
stories.background: India and the US have been negotiating a broader trade agreement for over a year, aiming to cut tariffs and expand market access for goods on both sides. In **February 2026**, Presidents Trump and Modi jointly announced they'd reached a deal lowering US tariffs on Indian exports from 25% to 18% — but that was described as a first step, not the final comprehensive agreement both sides say they still want. Since then, momentum on the full interim agreement has been slower than expected, with earlier reports in the summer describing prospects as **'dimming'** ahead of an August 1 informal deadline that passed without a deal.
stories.what_happened: At the Ministry of External Affairs' regular briefing on Tuesday, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told reporters that the **conversation between India and the US on the interim bilateral trade agreement is ongoing**, and that both governments have done substantial work toward finalizing it. He did not give a specific timeline for when a deal might be signed. This comes even as, separately, a coalition of **25 Democratic-led US states** has sued the Trump administration over a different set of tariffs — measures that place India in a 10% bracket — arguing they exceed the president's legal authority.
stories.why_it_matters: Tariff levels directly affect how competitively priced Indian exports (textiles, pharmaceuticals, IT services, engineering goods) are in the massive US market, so every month of delay matters for exporters and the companies that employ them. The lawsuit over the broader tariffs also adds legal uncertainty on top of the negotiation delay — even a signed deal with India could be complicated by a separate court fight over the underlying US tariff authority.
stories.ripple_effects: Indian exporters and US importers are left planning around uncertainty rather than a locked-in tariff rate. If the US courts eventually strike down the broader tariff program, it could reshape the leverage both sides have in the India-specific talks.
stories.why_now: The MEA statement came at its routine Tuesday briefing, and follows a summer in which reports repeatedly described the interim deal's prospects as fading past informal deadlines.
stories.watch_next: Whether India and the US name a firm date to sign the interim agreement, and how the 25-state tariff lawsuit proceeds through US courts.

key_terms.definition: A partial trade deal meant to lock in some tariff cuts and market access now, ahead of a fuller, more complete agreement later.

stories.the_lesson: Trade deals announced with fanfare at the leader-to-leader level often still take many more months of technical negotiation before they're actually final — the handshake photo is rarely the finish line.
stories.market_link: Indian exporters to the US (textiles, IT services, pharma, engineering goods) are directly affected by the eventual tariff rate this negotiation locks in.

stories.title: Government's ₹31,400 crore LIC share sale is oversubscribed 3.3 times by institutions — but the stock still tumbles 8.7%
key_points: The government offered to sell up to **6.5% of its stake in LIC**, India's largest state-owned insurer, through an **Offer for Sale (OFS)**.
The **institutional portion was oversubscribed 3.32 times**, with bids worth **₹36,400 crore** pouring in against the base offer.
The government **exercised its 'greenshoe' option** to sell an extra 4%, taking the total offer to **822.25 million shares**.
The floor price was set at **₹382 a share**, a **10.8% discount** to Monday's closing price — and LIC's stock fell **8.7% to ₹391.30** on the news.
Even after the full sale, the **government will still own about 90%** of LIC, down from its current 96.5% stake.
stories.background: LIC (Life Insurance Corporation of India) is India's largest insurer and one of its most valuable state-owned companies, and the government has been gradually **selling down its stake** over several years — partly to meet stock-exchange rules that require large listed companies to have a minimum public shareholding, and partly to raise revenue for the budget. An 'Offer for Sale' is a mechanism that lets a company's existing large shareholder — here, the government — sell shares directly on the stock exchange without issuing new ones. A 'greenshoe option' lets the seller sell additional shares beyond the original plan if demand is strong enough.
stories.what_happened: The Indian government launched an OFS to sell up to **6.5% of its stake in LIC**, worth roughly **₹31,400 crore** at the floor price of **₹382 per share** — a price set at a **10.8% discount** to the previous day's closing price to attract buyers. The non-retail (institutional) portion of the offer was **oversubscribed 3.32 times on the opening day**, with bids worth **₹36,400 crore**, prompting the government to exercise its **greenshoe option** and expand the total sale to **822.25 million shares**. Despite the strong institutional demand, LIC's stock price fell sharply, dropping **8.7% to close at ₹391.30** on the NSE, as the market absorbed the discount and the dilution of government ownership. Even after the entire stake sale goes through, the **Centre will still hold close to 90%** of LIC.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest government stake sales of the year and a key piece of the Centre's **disinvestment** strategy — using proceeds from selling shares in state-run companies to help fund the budget. Strong institutional demand shows big investors still see value in LIC, even though retail shareholders are watching the stock price fall on the news.
stories.ripple_effects: The extra free-float (shares available for public trading) from this sale could eventually help LIC's weighting in major stock indices, potentially prompting index funds to buy more of the stock over time. It also adds to government revenue this fiscal year, which can ease pressure on the **fiscal deficit** — the gap between what the government spends and what it earns.
stories.why_now: The OFS opened and was oversubscribed today, with the government's greenshoe decision and the stock's reaction also playing out today.
stories.watch_next: Whether the retail portion of the OFS (opening after the institutional book) also sees strong demand, and how LIC's stock performs once the sale is fully settled.

key_terms.definition: A way for a company's big existing shareholder to sell shares directly on the stock exchange to the public, without the company itself issuing new shares.
A pre-arranged right that lets the seller in a share sale offer more shares than originally planned if investor demand is strong.
The government selling its ownership stake in a state-run company, usually to raise revenue or meet listing rules.

stories.the_lesson: A share sale can be a 'success' by the numbers — oversubscribed, extra shares sold — and still send the stock price down, because a lower discounted price plus more shares in circulation can outweigh investor enthusiasm in the short term.
stories.market_link: LIC (NSE/BSE-listed) shares fell 8.7% on the news; the OFS also affects LIC's weighting in Nifty/Sensex-tracking index funds going forward.

stories.title: Tamil Nadu's opposition leader Udhayanidhi Stalin is arrested from his Chennai home, then ordered released by the Madras High Court
key_points: **Udhayanidhi Stalin**, DMK leader and **Leader of the Opposition in Tamil Nadu**, was arrested from his **Neelankarai residence in Chennai on Tuesday morning** by Thanjavur police.
The arrest stems from an **FIR in Thanjavur** over alleged derogatory remarks he made about actor **Trisha Krishnan** during a farmers' protest over Cauvery water.
The FIR invokes sections covering **harassment of women, hate speech, IT Act violations, and provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** — India's newer criminal code.
The **Madras High Court ordered his release** after questioning, directing him to cooperate with the ongoing investigation.
The **DMK has called the case politically motivated**, or a 'false case,' and staged protests against the arrest.
stories.background: Udhayanidhi Stalin is the son of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister **M.K. Stalin** and a senior DMK leader who currently holds the position of **Leader of the Opposition** in the state assembly, following a change in Tamil Nadu's political alignment. Tamil Nadu has been gripped by tension over **Cauvery river water sharing with Karnataka**, which has triggered farmer protests in the state. The complaint against Udhayanidhi originated from the women's wing of the ruling **Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)** party, alleging he made offensive remarks about actor Trisha Krishnan while addressing one such protest.
stories.what_happened: A team of **Thanjavur police personnel arrested Udhayanidhi Stalin** from his residence in Neelankarai, Chennai, on **Tuesday morning, August 4**, and took him to Thanjavur for questioning. The case originated from an FIR filed at **Thanjavur East Police Station**, based on a complaint from the organiser of the ruling TVK party's women's wing, accusing him of derogatory remarks about actor Trisha Krishnan made during a farmers' protest over Cauvery water sharing. The FIR cites sections related to **harassment of women, hate speech, the IT Act, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita**. After he was taken in for questioning, the **Madras High Court intervened and ordered his release**, while directing him to continue cooperating with the investigation. The DMK has pushed back hard, calling the case a politically motivated 'false case' and organizing protests against what it calls a targeted arrest of its senior leader.
stories.why_it_matters: The arrest of a sitting **Leader of the Opposition** — and the chief minister's own son — is a major flashpoint in Tamil Nadu politics, especially given the backdrop of an already-tense Cauvery water dispute. It raises questions about whether state police powers are being used for political ends, a recurring and sensitive theme in India's state-versus-centre and party-versus-party battles.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect this to sharpen political rhetoric between the DMK and the ruling TVK ahead of future elections, with both sides using the episode to paint the other as authoritarian or lawless. It could also affect the broader **Cauvery water-sharing tensions**, since the original protest that triggered the remarks is itself part of an unresolved dispute between Tamil Nadu and Karnataka.
stories.why_now: The arrest happened this morning, and the Madras High Court's release order followed within hours, making this a fast-moving, same-day story.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Thanjavur police pursue further legal action against Udhayanidhi Stalin despite the release order, and how the DMK-TVK political clash over this incident develops.

key_terms.definition: India's newer criminal code that replaced the colonial-era Indian Penal Code in 2024, covering offenses like hate speech and harassment.
The formal head of the largest opposition party in a legislature, with certain institutional rights and privileges.

stories.the_lesson: In Indian state politics, a single FIR can escalate within hours into a major arrest-and-release drama involving a top leader — showing how quickly local police action can become a full-blown political confrontation.

stories.title: Two firefighters die when a wall collapses while battling a blaze at a Greater Noida chip factory
key_points: A fire broke out late Monday night at **ILGIM**, an electronics chip manufacturing unit in Greater Noida's **Ecotech-3 industrial area**.
A **wall and iron beam collapsed** on firefighters while they worked to douse the blaze, killing **2 and injuring 3 more**.
The two firefighters killed were identified as **Tirthpal Singh and Rohit Yadav**.
At least **six fire brigade vehicles** were rushed to the site once the blaze was reported.
The three injured firefighters are reported to be in **stable condition**.
stories.background: Greater Noida's **Ecotech-3** is a dense industrial zone housing electronics and manufacturing units on the outskirts of Delhi. Factory fires are a recurring hazard in India's rapidly built industrial parks, where structural safety standards and fire-response infrastructure can lag the pace of construction. Firefighters battling factory blazes routinely face risks beyond the fire itself, including structural collapse in buildings not designed to withstand prolonged heat and water exposure.
stories.what_happened: Late on the night of **August 3**, a fire broke out at **ILGIM**, an electronics chip manufacturing company in the Ecotech-3 industrial area of Greater Noida, Uttar Pradesh. At least **six fire brigade vehicles** were dispatched once the blaze was reported. While firefighters were working to put out the fire, a **wall and an iron beam inside the factory suddenly collapsed**, striking five of the firefighters. **Tirthpal Singh and Rohit Yadav died** in the collapse, while the other three injured personnel are in stable condition and being treated.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a fatal reminder that industrial firefighting carries structural-collapse risk on top of the fire itself, especially in factories that may not meet robust building codes. Firefighter deaths in the line of duty typically trigger scrutiny of both the specific factory's safety compliance and broader industrial fire-safety enforcement in fast-growing zones like Greater Noida.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect Uttar Pradesh authorities to order a safety inspection of the ILGIM facility and potentially other units in Ecotech-3, and for the fire department to review protocols for entering buildings with unclear structural integrity during a blaze. The firefighters' deaths may also renew calls for better protective equipment and hazard training for India's municipal fire services.
stories.why_now: The story is breaking today as authorities confirm the deaths and begin assessing what caused the structural collapse during the firefighting operation.
stories.watch_next: Whether an official inquiry finds the factory violated fire-safety or structural codes, and what compensation or safety measures the state government announces for the firefighters' families and the fire department.
stories.the_lesson: Firefighters battling an industrial blaze face a second, often less visible danger — structural collapse from heat- and water-weakened buildings — which is why fire services increasingly train specifically for collapse risk, not just for extinguishing flames.

stories.title: Delhi Police stop Kejriwal's march to PM Modi's residence over E20 ethanol-blended petrol
key_points: **Arvind Kejriwal** and about **100 AAP supporters** tried to march to **PM Modi's residence** to hand over petitions against **E20 petrol**.
They carried more than **2.3 lakh (230,000) petitions** collected from citizens nationwide opposing the ethanol-blended fuel policy.
**Delhi Police stopped the march** on Firoz Shah Road, deploying heavy security including paramilitary forces.
Former Delhi deputy CM **Manish Sisodia** and AAP's **Jasmine Shah** sat down in protest after being blocked.
Kejriwal vowed to **intensify the campaign** against the Centre's E20 policy rather than back down.
stories.background: **E20 petrol** is petrol blended with **20% ethanol**, part of the central government's push to cut oil imports and vehicle emissions by mixing biofuel into every litre sold at the pump. AAP, which lost power in Delhi but remains a vocal opposition force, has campaigned against the mandate, arguing ethanol-blended fuel **damages engines and reduces mileage** in older vehicles, a claim the government disputes. Kejriwal, AAP's national convenor, has increasingly used street marches and petition drives to keep pressure on the BJP-led central government since leaving Delhi's chief ministership.
stories.what_happened: On the morning of **August 4**, Arvind Kejriwal led roughly **100 AAP workers and leaders**, including Manish Sisodia and Jasmine Shah, on a march toward Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence. Their goal was to formally submit over **2.3 lakh petitions** gathered from citizens across India opposing the government's E20 ethanol-blended petrol policy, which they say is hurting vehicle owners. **Delhi Police intercepted and stopped the march** on Firoz Shah Road before it could reach the PM's residence, having deployed a heavy security presence of Delhi Police and paramilitary personnel in anticipation. Blocked from proceeding, Kejriwal and the other leaders **sat down in protest on the road**. Kejriwal said afterward that he would **intensify** the campaign against the E20 mandate rather than stand down.
stories.why_it_matters: It's a fresh flashpoint in the ongoing tension between AAP and the central government, and a real test of how much street pressure a fuel-policy complaint can generate when it's backed by a large, organized petition drive rather than just a party statement. It also keeps ethanol-blending policy — a genuine consumer cost-of-living issue for vehicle owners — in the national conversation.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect AAP to escalate with further protests or legal petitions if the government doesn't respond, and for the E20 debate to draw more public and possibly opposition-wide attention as a fuel-cost issue ahead of future state elections. It could also pressure the oil ministry to publicly defend or clarify the ethanol-blending program's effect on vehicles.
stories.why_now: AAP had been building this petition campaign for weeks; today's march was timed as the delivery point, escalating from petition-gathering to a direct, visible confrontation at the seat of power.
stories.watch_next: Whether Kejriwal announces a follow-up protest or legal action, and whether the central government issues any formal response to the E20 petitions.

key_terms.definition: Petrol blended with 20% ethanol (a plant-based biofuel), mandated by India to cut oil imports and emissions, though some argue it can affect fuel efficiency in older vehicles.

stories.the_lesson: A large, organized petition drive — not just a protest march — is a common opposition tactic to force a government response, because it demonstrates measurable public backing rather than just party messaging.

stories.title: BSE's profit more than doubles to ₹539 crore as India's exchange operator rides a derivatives and mutual-fund boom
key_points: **BSE Ltd's** consolidated profit jumped **103% year-on-year to ₹539 crore** in the June quarter.
Revenue climbed **59% to ₹1,045 crore**, driven by derivatives trading and mutual fund distribution.
Operating **EBITDA rose 122% to ₹626 crore**, with margins expanding to a strong **65%**.
Growth was fueled by **robust derivatives trading**, mutual-fund distribution, and BSE's international arm, **India INX**.
The results land the same week several other major Indian companies — Airtel, ONGC, ITC — are also reporting.
stories.background: BSE Ltd (formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange) is Asia's oldest stock exchange and, alongside the NSE, one of India's two dominant trading venues — it earns money by charging fees on every trade, especially the fast-growing options and futures ('derivatives') segment. Exchanges like BSE are effectively a bet on how much India trades: when retail and institutional investors are active, especially in high-frequency derivatives, exchange revenue rises sharply because fees scale with volume. India's derivatives market has exploded in size over the past few years, making exchange operators one of the more direct ways to track that boom's profitability.
stories.what_happened: BSE Ltd reported its April–June quarter (Q1 FY27) results on Tuesday, showing consolidated profit after tax surging **103% year-on-year to ₹539 crore**, up sharply from the same quarter last year. Consolidated revenue rose **59% to ₹1,045 crore**, while operating EBITDA — a measure of core operating profitability before interest, tax, and depreciation — jumped **122% to ₹626 crore**, pushing EBITDA margin to **65%**. The company credited the strong showing to robust derivatives trading volumes, its growing mutual-fund distribution business, and continued investment in its international arm, India INX, which operates out of Gujarat's GIFT City. BSE is scheduled to hold its earnings call with analysts and investors this evening.
stories.why_it_matters: BSE's numbers are a real-time read on how much money is moving through India's markets — a 65% margin and a doubling of profit signal that trading activity, especially in derivatives, remains extremely strong even as some earlier boom-era froth has cooled elsewhere in Indian markets. Because exchanges profit from volume rather than direction, this result says more about how *active* Indian markets are than whether they're going up or down.
stories.ripple_effects: Strong exchange earnings often draw regulatory attention, since SEBI (India's market regulator) has previously flagged concerns about retail investors losing money in options trading even as exchanges profit from that same volume. Investors will also watch whether rival NSE's eventual results echo the same derivatives-driven strength, which would confirm this is a market-wide trend rather than BSE-specific execution.
stories.why_now: BSE reported today as part of a broad wave of quarterly earnings from more than 130 Indian companies scheduled for release on August 4.
stories.watch_next: NSE's own quarterly results and commentary, and any SEBI commentary on retail derivatives trading volumes and investor losses.

key_terms.definition: Financial contracts like options and futures whose value is derived from an underlying asset (like a stock index) — they let traders bet on price moves without owning the asset, and exchanges earn a fee on every contract traded.

stories.the_lesson: A market exchange's profits track trading *volume*, not market direction — an exchange can post record earnings in a volatile or even falling market, because activity itself is what it gets paid for.
stories.market_link: BSE Ltd (NSE/BSE: BSE) shares are likely to react to the results; the print is also a bullish read-through for exchange-linked and brokerage stocks tied to Indian derivatives volumes.

stories.title: Rajya Sabha adjourned twice today as Kharge accuses the government of handing 70+ acres to the Ram Temple trust and demands Amit Shah explain the student crackdown
key_points: The **Rajya Sabha** (Parliament's upper house) was adjourned **twice on Tuesday**, till 2 pm, amid Opposition protests.
Congress president **Mallikarjun Kharge** alleged the government handed over **more than 70 acres of land** to the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust.
Kharge also demanded Home Minister **Amit Shah** personally explain the **police crackdown on students** during the July 20 Parliament march.
He asked pointedly where agencies like the **ED, CBI, and Income Tax department** were on the alleged land dealings.
Kharge, as Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha, was **not allowed to speak** on the matter before the House adjourned.
stories.background: The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust manages the Ram Temple in Ayodhya and has handled large volumes of land purchases and public donations since the temple's construction began. This clash follows weeks of Opposition anger over the **July 20 police crackdown on students** protesting the NEET-UG medical entrance exam paper leak at a Parliament march, which the Opposition has repeatedly tried to force the government to address on the floor of the House. The Rajya Sabha is Parliament's upper house, where laws are debated and the government is held to account through structured questioning — but sessions have been repeatedly disrupted this session by the same standoff.
stories.what_happened: The Rajya Sabha was adjourned twice on Tuesday, August 4, first and then again until 2 pm, as Opposition MPs pressed for a statement from Home Minister Amit Shah on two fronts: alleged police excesses against students during the July 20 protest march, and new allegations about land transfers to the Ram Temple trust. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge alleged the central government handed over **more than 70 acres of land** to the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust, and separately raised concerns about the management of cash donations and offerings made to the trust. He questioned aloud why investigative agencies — the Enforcement Directorate, CBI, and Income Tax department — had not scrutinized the matter, saying "those who loot in the name of Lord Ram should apologize to the entire country." As Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha, Kharge attempted to raise the issue formally but was not permitted to speak before the presiding officer adjourned the House amid the disruption.
stories.why_it_matters: This combines two politically charged threads — alleged financial impropriety around a religious institution central to the ruling party's identity, and unresolved anger over police conduct toward student protesters — into one parliamentary standoff that is now paralyzing normal legislative business. A demand for a home minister to answer publicly for police action is a significant accountability moment regardless of how it's ultimately resolved.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued adjournments eat into the limited days Parliament has each session to pass legislation and debate government policy, and repeated disruptions of this kind tend to harden partisan positions rather than resolve them. If the land-transfer allegations gain traction, they could pressure the government to either produce documentation rebutting Kharge's numbers or refer the matter to an investigative agency, which would keep the story alive for weeks.
stories.why_now: The Opposition had explicitly said a day earlier it would protest in Parliament today specifically to force a statement from Amit Shah, so today's disruption was a planned escalation, not a spontaneous one.
stories.watch_next: Whether the government responds directly to the 70-acre land allegation, and whether Amit Shah ultimately makes the demanded statement in either house of Parliament.

key_terms.definition: The formal title given to the head of the largest non-government party in a legislative house, with specific rights like being consulted on key appointments.

stories.the_lesson: In a parliamentary system, the Opposition's most basic power is often just the ability to disrupt business until it is heard — adjournments are a blunt but real form of leverage when a government controls the agenda.

stories.title: Pro-Kannada groups call a Karnataka-wide bandh for August 13 over a fresh order to release Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu
key_points: Over **1,600 Kannada organisations** have called for a bandh across Karnataka on **August 13**, from 6am to 6pm.
The trigger: a **Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA)** order directing Karnataka to release **3,500 cusecs of water daily to Tamil Nadu for 15 days**.
Activists argue Karnataka itself is facing **water scarcity** and that the release would hurt local farmers.
The **Kannada film industry** has publicly extended support to the bandh call.
This is the latest flashpoint in a **decades-old inter-state dispute** over sharing the Cauvery river's water.
stories.background: The Cauvery river dispute is one of India's oldest and most politically charged inter-state water conflicts, pitting Karnataka (upstream) against Tamil Nadu (downstream) over how much river water each state can use, mainly for irrigation and drinking supply. The Supreme Court eventually settled the sharing formula and created the **Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA)** to enforce it, but on-the-ground compliance remains a recurring flashpoint whenever water levels run low, and past bandh calls over the issue have shut down Bengaluru and other Karnataka cities before.
stories.what_happened: Pro-Kannada organisations have called for a statewide bandh (shutdown) in Karnataka on **August 13**, running from **6am to 6pm**, to protest a CWMA directive ordering the state to release **3,500 cusecs of Cauvery water per day to Tamil Nadu for 15 days**. Activist Vatal Nagaraj said the shutdown has the backing of more than **1,600 Kannada organisations** and over **1,000 other groups** across the state, arguing that Karnataka itself is short on water and that the release will hurt local farmers who depend on the same river for irrigation. The Kannada film industry has also thrown its support behind the bandh call. The protest adds to a summer already marked by heavy flooding and monsoon disruption elsewhere in Karnataka and neighboring states.
stories.why_it_matters: A statewide bandh can shut down transport, businesses, and daily life across Karnataka's cities including Bengaluru, India's tech hub — and the Cauvery dispute has a history of triggering real unrest, including past incidents where protesters targeted water infrastructure. It is also a recurring test of inter-state relations that periodically escalates into court battles.
stories.ripple_effects: A bandh could disrupt business operations, transport and daily commerce in Bengaluru and other Karnataka cities on August 13; it also raises the political temperature between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu's governments and could pressure the CWMA and central government to revisit the release order.
stories.why_now: The CWMA's fresh order to release water for 15 straight days, issued amid Karnataka's own reservoir concerns, is what triggered this specific bandh call — timed for one of the most contentious points in the annual water-sharing cycle.
stories.watch_next: Whether the CWMA revises or upholds its release order before August 13, and how large and disruptive the bandh actually turns out to be.

key_terms.definition: A unit measuring water flow — cubic feet per second — commonly used in India to describe how much river water is being released.

stories.the_lesson: Shared natural resources like rivers routinely become political flashpoints between neighboring states, especially when supply is tight — technical water-sharing formulas set by courts don't make the underlying scarcity, or the local anger over it, go away.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty snap their 4-day rally, closing lower as a late Nifty comeback trims the losses
key_points: Sensex fell **210 points to 78,428**; Nifty lost **159 points to 24,614.90** on Tuesday, August 4.
The drop **snaps a four-session winning streak** that had been driven by falling crude oil prices.
Markets opened higher — Sensex up nearly **494 points** — before **global caution** dragged indices down through the day.
Investors stayed wary of **Middle East tensions** and their knock-on effect on crude prices and the **rupee**.
**Trent, Bajaj Finance, BEL, Tata Steel** were among the gainers; **HUL, NTPC, HDFC Bank, RIL** led the losers.
stories.background: Indian benchmark indices had been on a rare four-session winning streak, lifted mainly by falling global crude oil prices — cheaper oil is good for India, which imports most of its oil, because it eases both inflation and the trade deficit. But that relief has been running into a countervailing risk: the escalating **US-Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz**, a chokepoint oil-tanker route, which threatens to push oil prices back up if the conflict disrupts shipping.
stories.what_happened: India's Sensex and Nifty closed lower on **Tuesday, August 4**, ending a four-day winning streak. The Sensex fell **210 points to 78,428.45**, and the Nifty dropped **159 points to 24,614.90**. The session had opened on a strong note, with the Sensex up nearly **494 points (0.62%)** at the open, but the gains faded through the day as investors turned cautious on mixed global cues. A late rally in the Nifty trimmed what would have been steeper losses. Stocks like **Trent, Bajaj Finance, BEL, Tata Steel, M&M, Bajaj Finserv and Titan** rose as much as **1.15%**, while **HUL, NTPC, HDFC Bank, Reliance Industries and IndiGo** fell as much as **1.7%**. Traders pointed to continued unease over Middle East geopolitical tensions and their potential to push crude oil prices — and the rupee — around.
stories.why_it_matters: The four-day rally had been one of the few genuinely positive threads in a market otherwise weighed down by a weak rupee and elevated oil prices from the Iran crisis; today's reversal shows how quickly that support can evaporate if global risk sentiment sours again.
stories.ripple_effects: A weaker market session adds pressure on an already-fragile rupee (already near record lows) and complicates the RBI's currency-defense efforts; it can also dent near-term sentiment for retail investors and IPO pricing if the pullback extends.
stories.why_now: Today's reversal tracks directly with renewed nervousness over the Israel-Iran/Strait of Hormuz standoff, which investors are watching closely because any disruption there could send oil prices — and India's import bill — sharply higher.
stories.watch_next: Whether Wednesday's session extends the pullback or the four-day uptrend resumes, and how crude oil prices move as the Iran situation develops.
stories.the_lesson: Markets that rally on one supportive factor (here, falling oil) remain fragile if a bigger risk (a Middle East oil-supply shock) is sitting right underneath it — a good week can reverse in a single session.
stories.market_link: Directly a Sensex/Nifty and rupee story; also linked to crude oil prices via the Iran/Strait of Hormuz standoff.

stories.title: Kerala's monsoon death toll climbs to 20 as red alert hits eight districts and thousands shelter in relief camps
key_points: Kerala's rain-related death toll has risen to **20** over the past three days, with search operations still underway for missing people.
A separate landslide in **Karnataka** killed **3 more**, taking the combined southern-India toll to at least **23**.
India's weather office has issued a **red alert in eight Kerala districts** today, with **Pathanamthitta and Kottayam** worst affected.
Nearly **7,700 people** have been moved into roughly **275 relief camps** across the state.
**Five dams** are on red alert and schools are shut in **10 districts** as rain continues.
stories.background: Kerala and coastal Karnataka have been under sustained monsoon pressure for days, with earlier reporting putting the combined toll at 11 in Kerala plus 3 in a Karnataka landslide. Heavy, continuous rain since has pushed the Kerala figure alone to 20, with authorities racing to evacuate low-lying and hillside areas before more landslides hit. Kerala's hilly terrain, saturated soil from repeated rain spells, and dense population near rivers and reservoirs make it especially exposed to compounding flood and landslide risk each monsoon season.
stories.what_happened: India's meteorological department issued a **red alert for eight Kerala districts today**, warning of continued heavy rainfall, as the state's rain-related death toll climbed to **20** over three days of monsoon fury. **Pathanamthitta and Kottayam** districts have been hit hardest, with flooding and landslides inundating homes and cutting off infrastructure. Authorities have moved roughly **7,700 people** into about **275 relief camps**, and **five dams** are now on red alert as reservoir levels rise. Educational institutions have been shut in **10 districts** as a precaution. In neighboring Karnataka, a separate landslide has killed **3 people**, bringing the combined death toll across the two states to at least **23**, with rescue and search operations continuing for people still missing.
stories.why_it_matters: A death toll nearly doubling in a matter of days, alongside dams reaching red-alert levels, signals the flood risk is still actively worsening rather than past its peak — meaning the human and infrastructure toll could keep climbing before this monsoon spell breaks.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued rain and reservoir stress raise the risk of controlled dam releases that could flood areas further downstream, and disrupted roads and rail lines in the worst-hit districts will squeeze the movement of relief supplies and emergency crews. Prolonged school closures and relief-camp stays also strain local administrations already stretched thin by repeated monsoon emergencies this season.
stories.why_now: The death toll and alert level are escalating today because the same rain system that caused the initial deaths days ago has continued largely uninterrupted, pushing already-saturated hillsides and near-full dams closer to their breaking point.
stories.watch_next: Whether the India Meteorological Department upgrades any of the red-alert districts further, and whether any of the five red-alert dams are forced into emergency water releases.

key_terms.definition: India's highest weather warning level, meaning extremely heavy rainfall is expected and authorities should take immediate action, including evacuations.

stories.the_lesson: In flood emergencies, the death toll and infrastructure strain (like dam levels) can keep rising for days after the initial disaster if the same weather system persists — the first reported numbers are rarely the final ones.

stories.title: India's rupee grinds toward record lows as the RBI keeps selling dollars to defend it
key_points: The rupee traded near **95.29 per dollar** on August 3 — down **over 8% in the past year**.
Traders say the **RBI intervened aggressively**, selling dollars to slow the currency's slide.
India's **forex reserves — the RBI's war chest** — have been falling as it defends the rupee.
The pressure is tied to **Trump's tariffs on Indian goods** and fears of rising oil prices from US-Iran tensions.
A weak rupee makes India's imports — especially **oil** — more expensive, feeding inflation.
stories.background: The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** doesn't fix the rupee's value, but it does step in — buying or selling dollars — to stop moves it sees as too sharp or disorderly. It has been under pressure for weeks: the US has layered fresh **tariffs on Indian exports** this year (part of a wider round of tariffs on dozens of countries), and Gulf tensions have kept a floor under oil prices, which matters hugely for India since it imports most of its crude.
stories.what_happened: The rupee was trading around **95.29 to the dollar** on August 3, down more than **8% over the past year**, even after a modest one-month recovery. Traders pointed to **continued RBI dollar-selling** to slow the decline, following what they described as aggressive intervention in the prior session. Market participants cautioned that further rupee strength could be capped if oil prices rebound amid the ongoing **US-Iran standoff**, since India imports the vast majority of the crude it consumes.
stories.why_it_matters: A weaker rupee raises the cost of everything India imports — oil, electronics, fertilizer — which feeds directly into consumer inflation and complicates the RBI's interest-rate decisions, including its rate-setting panel currently meeting this week.
stories.ripple_effects: Higher import costs squeeze margins for fuel retailers and import-heavy manufacturers, while IT and pharma exporters that earn in dollars get a modest boost. A shrinking reserves cushion also leaves the RBI with less room to defend the currency if pressure escalates further.
stories.why_now: Fresh US tariffs on Indian goods took effect this week, and renewed Gulf tensions are keeping oil prices elevated — both push the rupee lower at the same time the RBI is trying to hold the line.
stories.watch_next: The outcome of the RBI's ongoing 3-day rate-setting meeting, and whether the rupee tests fresh lows if oil prices climb further.

key_terms.definition: The foreign currency (mostly US dollars) a country's central bank holds in reserve — used, among other things, to buy or sell in the market to support its own currency's value.

stories.the_lesson: When a central bank defends its currency by selling dollars, it's spending a finite war chest — how fast reserves fall is a real-time gauge of how much strain a currency is actually under.
stories.market_link: A weaker rupee raises costs for oil marketing companies and import-heavy sectors, while giving IT and pharma exporters a modest tailwind.

stories.title: South Gujarat is under water: Valsad gets a metre of rain in 24 hours as NDRF scrambles
key_points: **Valsad district** recorded over **100 centimetres of rain in just 24 hours**.
The **IMD issued fresh red alerts** across multiple South Gujarat districts as monsoon activity intensifies.
Rivers are rising in **Navsari and Surat**, triggering significant urban flooding in low-lying areas.
**NDRF teams deployed** for rescue operations; schools and colleges shut for safety.
Forecasters warn of **heavy rain for another 18 hours**, with landslide watches for Dang and Tapi.
stories.background: India's economy and daily life run on the **southwest monsoon**, the seasonal rains that arrive from June to September and deliver most of the country's annual rainfall. Gujarat had already reported **flooding deaths and evacuations in the last week of July/early August** as heavy rain battered the state. Early August is typically a peak-intensity stretch of the monsoon, and this year's rains have already triggered major flooding in Kerala, Assam, and now Gujarat.
stories.what_happened: South Gujarat is facing a severe deluge, with **Valsad district recording over 100 centimetres of rainfall in a single 24-hour period** — an extreme, cloudburst-level total. The India Meteorological Department issued fresh **red alerts** for multiple districts as the rain intensified. Rivers are rising fast in **Navsari and Surat**, causing significant urban flooding in low-lying neighborhoods. State authorities have deployed the **National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)** for rescue operations, and local administrations shut schools and colleges as a precaution. Forecasters expect heavy rain to continue for roughly another 18 hours, with **Dang and Tapi districts under watch for landslides**.
stories.why_it_matters: Extreme, concentrated rainfall like this overwhelms drainage and river systems built for average conditions, putting lives, homes, and infrastructure at risk in a short window rather than gradually.
stories.ripple_effects: Crop damage in Gujarat's farm belt, transport and supply-chain disruption as roads and rail flood, and a rising toll on insurers and state disaster-relief budgets. It adds to a national picture — Kerala and Assam are already dealing with deadly flooding this monsoon season.
stories.why_now: Early August sits at the peak-intensity stretch of the southwest monsoon, when moisture-laden weather systems regularly dump extreme rainfall totals over short windows in western and central India.
stories.watch_next: Whether rainfall eases within the forecast 18-hour window, and whether the death toll or evacuation numbers rise as authorities complete rescue operations.
stories.the_lesson: Monsoon flooding often arrives as short, intense bursts rather than steady rain — a single day's extreme rainfall (sometimes called a cloudburst) can overwhelm infrastructure that copes fine with an average monsoon.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty close up for a 4th straight session as falling crude oil keeps lifting Indian markets

thread.previously: We reported that the Sensex opened up 788.7 points and the Nifty added 189 points to cross 24,550 on the morning of August 3, driven by falling crude oil prices after the US held off on new Iran strikes, with markets also positioning ahead of the RBI's August 5 rate decision.
thread.changed: By the close of trading on August 3, some of that morning surge had faded, but the Sensex still finished up 544 points at 78,639.03 and the Nifty closed above 24,750 (up 390.70 points) — marking a 4th consecutive winning session, still powered by the same falling crude oil tailwind.

key_points: The **Sensex closed up 544.39 points (0.7%)** at **78,639.03**; the **Nifty 50 gained 390.70 points (1.60%)** to close at **24,774.30**.
It's the **4th straight winning session** for both benchmark indices.
**Falling crude oil prices** remained the single biggest driver, since India imports over 80% of its oil.
The **IT sector led gains**, with the Nifty IT index up over **3%** on the day.
Markets are now positioning ahead of the **RBI's rate decision on August 5**, where most economists expect the repo rate to stay unchanged at **5.25%**.
stories.background: India imports more than **80% of the crude oil** it uses, so global oil prices move Indian markets almost as directly as domestic company news — cheaper oil lowers the country's import bill, eases inflation, and boosts margins for oil-consuming businesses like airlines and paint makers. Oil prices have been falling as fears of a Middle East supply shock from the Iran conflict have eased in recent days. Meanwhile, India's central bank, the **RBI**, is in the middle of a **3-day Monetary Policy Committee meeting** (August 3–5) that will decide whether to change the **repo rate** — the interest rate at which it lends to banks, which ripples through to loan and deposit rates across the economy.
stories.what_happened: India's benchmark stock indices extended their rally through the close of trading on **Monday, August 3**: the **Sensex ended up 544.39 points (0.7%) at 78,639.03**, and the **Nifty 50 climbed 390.70 points (1.60%) to close at 24,774.30**, giving both indices their **fourth consecutive day of gains**. The rally moderated somewhat from the morning's sharper 788-point Sensex jump, but held up through the session on continued **crude oil price weakness**. **IT stocks led the advance**, with the sector index up more than 3% on the day, while investors also positioned ahead of the **RBI's rate decision**, due Wednesday, August 5, where a Reuters poll of 72 economists found 68 expect the repo rate to stay unchanged at **5.25%**.
stories.why_it_matters: A four-day winning streak, on top of a >500-point single-day gain, signals that foreign and domestic investors are growing more confident that the worst of the Middle East-driven oil price spike is behind markets — a meaningful sentiment shift after weeks of tariff- and oil-driven selling pressure on Indian equities.
stories.ripple_effects: A sustained rally tends to draw more foreign institutional investment back into Indian equities, and cheaper oil helps the rupee and eases inflation — both of which factor into the RBI's rate decision on Wednesday. IT stocks' outperformance also reflects renewed optimism about the sector heading into the back half of the year.
stories.why_now: The rally is riding continued declines in crude oil prices tied to de-escalating Middle East tensions, right as markets look ahead to the RBI's closely watched rate decision in two days.
stories.watch_next: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee decision on August 5, where the repo rate is widely expected to hold at 5.25% for a fourth straight time.

key_terms.definition: The interest rate at which India's central bank (the RBI) lends money to commercial banks — a key lever that influences loan and deposit rates across the economy.

stories.the_lesson: Stock market gains built on falling oil prices can fade as the trading day goes on — the morning's headline jump is often bigger than what actually survives to the closing bell, so the close, not the open, is the number that matters.
stories.market_link: Nifty IT stocks and oil-import-sensitive sectors (aviation, paints, tyres) were the biggest beneficiaries of the rally.

stories.title: BCCI names uncapped pacer Auqib Nabi as Jasprit Bumrah's replacement for India's Sri Lanka Test series
key_points: **Auqib Nabi**, an uncapped fast bowler, has been added to India's squad in place of **Jasprit Bumrah**.
Bumrah is still managing **discomfort in his left knee**, an injury from an ODI against England in Cardiff.
He's been rehabbing at the **BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru**, but recovery has taken longer than hoped.
The two-Test series against **Sri Lanka begins August 15 at Galle**.
There had been talk of Bumrah returning for the **second Test in Colombo**, but that's now ruled out.
stories.background: Jasprit Bumrah is India's premier fast bowler and one of the best in the world, so any extended absence is a significant blow to India's bowling attack. He picked up a left-knee injury while fielding during a one-day international against England in Cardiff in July, and had been working to recover in time for at least part of India's upcoming Test tour of Sri Lanka.
stories.what_happened: The BCCI has confirmed that uncapped fast bowler **Auqib Nabi** will replace Jasprit Bumrah in India's squad for the **two-Test series in Sri Lanka**, which starts August 15 at Galle. Bumrah is continuing to experience discomfort in his left knee, the injury he sustained fielding in an ODI against England in Cardiff, and has been rehabilitating at the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru. While there had been discussion about him potentially being fit for the second Test in Colombo, team medical staff have advised against rushing his return, ending any chance of him featuring in this series at all.
stories.why_it_matters: Losing Bumrah for an entire series removes India's most potent wicket-taking threat, forcing the team to rely on a less experienced pace attack against a Sri Lankan side playing at home. For Auqib Nabi, it's a high-pressure opportunity to make his Test debut standing in for the best bowler in the side.
stories.ripple_effects: India's bowling plans and team balance for the series will likely shift toward more responsibility for spin and the other pace bowlers in the squad. It also raises questions about Bumrah's workload management ahead of bigger assignments later in the year, given how often knee and back issues have interrupted his career.
stories.why_now: The BCCI finalized and announced the squad now because the Sri Lanka tour begins August 15, and a decision on Bumrah's fitness could not be delayed any further without disrupting team preparation.
stories.watch_next: Auqib Nabi's Test debut performance if selected, and any update on Bumrah's recovery timeline ahead of India's next Test assignment.
stories.the_lesson: For a team built heavily around one star performer, that player's absence doesn't just remove their output — it forces the whole game plan to change, testing depth that often only gets noticed when it's needed.

stories.title: Pakistan take a 43-run first-innings lead over West Indies after bowling them out for 344 in the series-deciding Trinidad Test
key_points: Pakistan bowled West Indies out for **344**, with spinner **Sajid Khan taking 4 for 85**.
That gives Pakistan a **43-run first-innings lead**, having earlier posted **387 all out**.
West Indies' innings was built on **Justin Greaves' 73** and **Roston Chase's 70**.
The match is the **series decider** — West Indies lead 1-0 after winning the series opener by 90 runs.
Day 4 forecasts **long sunny periods with a few isolated showers** at Queen's Park Oval.
stories.background: This is the **second and final Test** of Pakistan's tour of the West Indies, played at the historic **Queen's Park Oval** in Port of Spain, Trinidad, from August 2-6. West Indies enter this match with an **unassailable psychological edge** on paper, having won the first Test by 90 runs to take a 1-0 series lead — meaning Pakistan must win this Test just to draw the series.
stories.what_happened: Pakistan, who had earlier posted **387 all out** in their first innings (built on Saud Shafique's 160 and Babar Azam's contribution, despite Jomel Warrican's six-wicket haul), bowled West Indies out for **344** to take a **43-run first-innings lead**. West Indies' reply was anchored by **Justin Greaves (73)** and **Roston Chase (70)**, but Pakistan's spinner **Sajid Khan** cut through the middle and lower order to finish with **4 for 85**. With the match evenly poised heading into day 4, weather forecasts point to mostly sunny conditions with only brief interruptions, meaning a full day's play — and a result — remains likely.
stories.why_it_matters: Because West Indies already lead the two-match series 1-0, Pakistan must win this Test to square the series — a draw or West Indies win ends it in the hosts' favor. A 43-run lead going into the second innings puts Pakistan in the stronger position to force that result, but Test matches this close can still swing on a single session.
stories.ripple_effects: A Pakistan win would end their tour with a drawn series rather than a series loss, which matters for team morale and rankings points heading into their next assignments. For West Indies, holding on to win the series would be a significant confidence boost for a team that has struggled for consistency in recent years.
stories.why_now: This is the natural next-day update in an ongoing, live Test match — the first-innings lead was only established when West Indies' innings ended on day 3/4 of the five-day match.
stories.watch_next: Pakistan's second-innings batting effort and whether they can set a target big enough to bowl West Indies out twice inside the remaining two days.

key_terms.definition: In a Test match (where each side bats twice), the runs one team is ahead by after both sides have completed their first innings — a key advantage heading into the match's second half.

stories.the_lesson: In Test cricket, a first-innings lead is an advantage, not a guarantee — with two days left and conditions changing, the team ahead still has to bat and bowl well twice more to close it out.

thread.previously: Saud Shafique's 160 and Jomel Warrican's six-wicket haul had Pakistan holding a slender lead as their first innings wrapped up, with the Trinidad Test finely poised.
thread.changed: West Indies have now been bowled out for 344 in reply, with Sajid Khan's 4-85 turning Pakistan's slender edge into a clearer 43-run first-innings lead.

stories.title: Ben Stokes says his 'only worry is Joe' as Root returns to the England Test captaincy he quit in 2022
key_points: Ben Stokes has **retired as England Test captain** following the New Zealand series, handing the reins back to **Joe Root**.
Stokes says his only concern is that the captaincy affects Root the way it did when Root **gave up the job in 2022**.
He also questioned why vice-captain **Harry Brook** wasn't promoted to the role instead of Root.
New head coach **Stephen Fleming** has been appointed, replacing **Brendon McCullum** as Test coach.
Root begins his second stint as full-time captain against **Pakistan at Headingley on August 19**.
stories.background: Joe Root captained England's Test team from 2021 to 2022 before stepping down, saying the pressure of the job was affecting his own batting form and mental well-being; Ben Stokes then took over and, alongside coach Brendon McCullum, transformed England's approach with the aggressive 'Bazball' style of play. Stokes has now stepped away from the captaincy himself, and rather than promoting a new candidate, England has turned back to Root for a second stint in the role — a decision that has drawn mixed reactions given how the first spell ended.
stories.what_happened: Ben Stokes, who retired as England's Test captain after the New Zealand series, spoke publicly about Root's reappointment and voiced real concerns about it. He said his worry is that the captaincy could affect Root the same way it did in 2022, when the pressure of the job contributed to Root stepping down, adding that Root 'always put the team first; he always came second' during his own time as captain. Stokes also questioned why the selectors didn't instead promote vice-captain Harry Brook into the top job. Despite the concerns, Stokes said 'I love Rooty, I wish him nothing but success' and hopes he 'goes on and achieves amazing things' in the role. Separately, England confirmed Stephen Fleming as the new Test head coach, replacing Brendon McCullum, who has left international coaching. Stokes also said he would 'absolutely' like to coach England himself one day. Root's second stint as full-time Test captain formally begins against Pakistan at Headingley on August 19.
stories.why_it_matters: How England manages the psychological load on Root — the exact issue that ended his first captaincy — will shape both his individual form and the team's stability heading into a demanding Test calendar.
stories.ripple_effects: If Root struggles under the captaincy again, England may face renewed pressure to find an alternative leader (with Brook as the most obvious candidate); Fleming's appointment as coach also signals a tactical shift after the McCullum 'Bazball' era.
stories.why_now: Stokes' Test retirement and Fleming's coaching appointment have just been finalized, with Root's first match in charge now on the calendar for August 19 against Pakistan.
stories.watch_next: Root's first Test back as captain, against Pakistan at Headingley starting August 19, as the first real test of how he handles the role differently the second time around.

key_terms.definition: In cricket, the Test captain typically also bats or bowls at a high level while also handling tactics, media duties and team management — a dual burden that has visibly affected several players' individual form over the years.

stories.the_lesson: Leadership roles can carry a real personal cost even for elite performers — reappointing someone to a job that previously wore them down only works if the surrounding support (coaching, workload, delegation) genuinely changes this time.

stories.title: Shafique's 160 and Warrican's six-for set up a tense finish as Pakistan take a slender lead over West Indies in Trinidad
key_points: Pakistan were bowled out for **387**, taking a **43-run first-innings lead** over West Indies' 344.
Opener **Abdullah Shafique** anchored the innings with an unbeaten **160**, with **Babar Azam** adding 88.
West Indies spinner **Jomel Warrican** took **6 wickets for 112 runs**, keeping the hosts firmly in the contest.
Pakistan then took **three West Indies wickets** late on Day 3, swinging momentum back their way going into Day 4.
Pakistan arrive at this Test on an **eight-match losing streak away from home** — a run they're now well placed to end.
stories.background: Pakistan have historically struggled overseas, and this tour of the West Indies has been no exception — the tourists came into this second Test on the back of eight consecutive away losses. The two-Test series is being played at Port of Spain's Queen's Park Oval, with West Indies looking to build on home advantage while Pakistan search for a rare away win to end their long losing run.
stories.what_happened: West Indies were bowled out for 344 on Day 2 (Justin Greaves 73, captain Roston Chase 70), before Pakistan's reply was built around a commanding unbeaten 160 from opener Abdullah Shafique and 88 from Babar Azam, taking the tourists to 387 all out and a 43-run first-innings lead. West Indies left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican was the standout bowler for the hosts, taking 6 wickets for 112 runs to prevent Pakistan from running away with the innings. With West Indies batting again in their second innings, Pakistan struck three times late in the day's play, leaving the match finely balanced heading into Day 4 of the five-day Test (August 2-6).
stories.why_it_matters: This result will go a long way toward determining whether Pakistan can finally end their eight-match run without an away win — a genuine test of the team's ability to perform outside home conditions.
stories.ripple_effects: A Pakistan win would ease pressure on the team's away-form troubles and boost confidence ahead of future overseas assignments; a West Indies recovery would extend the hosts' competitiveness in a series they'll want to close out at home.
stories.why_now: This is Day 3 of a live, ongoing Test match (August 2-6) at Queen's Park Oval, with the result still very much in the balance.
stories.watch_next: How West Indies' second innings unfolds on Day 4 — whether Pakistan's bowlers can build on their late breakthroughs to set up a run-chase or a declaration-forcing lead.
